title: 1.3.5 Why Documentation Matters
description: One paragraph on why documentation matters in real software work, with a specific example. AI-graded with hints.

aiGrader.prompt:
Everything you need is in 1.3.4 (Comments) — go back and reread it if you get stuck. One paragraph is plenty, in your own everyday words.

Documentation means the comments inside the code, plus notes like a README that explain what the code does and how to use it.

Explain why documentation matters when people build software together. (1.3.4)

Your paragraph needs one specific example. Any of these work:
- A messy program you had to read, and the comments it did or did not have.
- A program of your own that you came back to later and had trouble following.
- A hypothetical: a teammate — or you, six months from now — opens this code with no documentation at all. What goes wrong, and how would documentation have prevented it?

The one thing that will not be enough is a general "documentation is good because it helps" with no concrete example attached.

rubric.title: Clear explanation of why documentation matters
rubric.description: Student gives a real reason documentation matters in professional work — e.g., other people (or future-you) have to read and maintain the code, onboarding new teammates, remembering intent months later, reducing bugs from misunderstanding. Full credit for a clear, correct reason in their own words. Deny if the answer is empty, off-topic, or only restates 'documentation is important' with no reasoning.

rubric.title: One specific, non-generic example
rubric.description: Student includes a concrete example — their A3.1 refactor, a specific messy-code experience, or a fleshed-out hypothetical with an actual scenario (who reads the code, what breaks without docs). Full credit requires specificity. Deny for vague hand-waving like 'for example it helps people' with no actual situation described.

rubric.title: Clear writing, one paragraph
rubric.description: The response is a coherent paragraph and is easy to read. Deny this criterion only for significant issues: a single sentence with no real content, or writing too disorganized to follow. Do not deny for length.
